title: The Travelling Church, 1781
summary: In 1781 Rev. Lewis Craig led about 200 Baptists and 400 other settlers from Spotsylvania County, Virginia, as the Travelling Church to Gilbert’s Creek.
bodyMarkdown:
In 1781 a whole Baptist congregation left Spotsylvania County, Virginia, for the Kentucky District. The [Travelling Church](https://grokipedia.com/page/the_travelling_church) was the largest group to move to the area in a single body. It was led by the Rev. Lewis Craig, one of three preacher sons of Toliver Craig Sr.

## Why they left

Baptists in colonial Virginia faced discrimination from the established Anglican church. The emigrants sought both religious freedom and fertile land. Craig saw the trek across the mountains as a parallel to the Israelites leaving Egypt for Canaan.

The group was more than a single church. Its core was most of Craig's Upper Spotsylvania congregation, and other settlers joined along the way. The emigrants also included people enslaved by the Craigs and other families.

## How many went

Accounts of its size differ. One account, the 1947 state historical marker, says Craig led his entire congregation of 200 Baptists and 400 other settlers. Another puts the group at "perhaps five or six hundred" people.

## The road west

The party walked down the Great Wagon Road through the Blue Ridge, past present-day Lynchburg, Roanoke and Fort Chiswell. It then joined the Wilderness Road and crossed the mountains at [Cumberland Gap](/stories/thomas-walker-and-cumberland-gap/) in the fall and winter of 1781. Capt. William Ellis guided the train, and only a little loss of life occurred on the frozen route.

Other preachers made the trip too. They included Lewis Craig's younger brother, the Rev. Joseph Craig, and Peter Durrett, an enslaved man who later became a pioneering Black minister in Lexington. Another brother, the Rev. Elijah Craig, stayed in Virginia for a while to help James Madison secure religious liberty, then followed.

## Gilbert's Creek

The group arrived at Gilbert's Creek in December 1781, in what is now Garrard County near [Lancaster](/stories/lancaster-at-wallaces-crossroads/). On a hilltop they built a fortified blockhouse that served as both a church and a defense against Native attacks. Across the road beside the creek, they raised a wooden stockade called Craig's Station, where the settlers lived.

About two years later, Craig and others moved farther north. The original congregation took the name Gilbert's Creek Baptist Church. It is the third-oldest Baptist church in Kentucky.

## Churches across the Bluegrass

Members of the Travelling Church went on to found many congregations. They include Forks of Dix River Church (1782), South Elkhorn Christian Church (1783), Clear Creek Baptist Church (1785) and First African Baptist Church (about 1790). One of their churches was the first north of the Kentucky River.

## Kentucky today

Gilbert's Creek Baptist Church still holds services, though it has moved a short distance from the original site. State Marker 25 stands on KY 39 southeast of Lancaster, and a monument marks the hilltop where the fortified church stood.
